authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Lynch brings Mt. Silver back, and Blackthorn never gets the last possession
articles.dek: Garshawn Lynch rushes for 145 yards and two touchdowns as the Reds reverse a 14–7 deficit, win 21–14 and earn a conference-title rematch with Saffron.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Garshawn Lynch had seventeen carries to make his argument. By the time Mt. Silver finished its final possession, Blackthorn had no remaining opportunity to answer it. The Reds won 21–14, recovered from a seven-point third-quarter deficit and advanced to host Saffron in the Kanto–Johto championship. Lynch supplied 145 rushing yards, two touchdowns and the recurring problem that kept the Dragons’ defense on the field while Hatterene waited on the sideline.

I was the only member of our five-writer panel to pick Mt. Silver this week. I mention that because four colleagues are currently preparing explanations of considerable length. The Reds had lost the regular-season meeting 30–22, their quarterback injuries were real, and Blackthorn had just scored five passing touchdowns at Cinnabar. Those were sound reasons to expect a difficult afternoon. Mt. Silver supplied one for itself, then found the players and possessions required to survive it.

The comeback belonged to more than the leading runner. Crem Ftzpatrik completed eighteen of twenty-five passes for 195 yards without an interception. Prinplup caught all four of his targets, including the third-down completion that sustained the winning touchdown drive. Scep Smith Jr. caught the deciding score after losing a fumble before halftime. The defense kept Blackthorn from converting two early recoveries into points and forced the final punt that allowed Lynch and Rat Grange to close the game.
Two lost fumbles and a manageable deficit

Mt. Silver reached halftime down 7–0 despite moving the ball into two possessions that ended in lost fumbles. Gregar Jenings caught a twenty-five-yard pass before fumbling to Blastoise at 3:54 of the second quarter. Later, Scep Smith Jr. lost the ball after a six-yard completion, with Politoed recovering. Blackthorn finished both ensuing possessions with punts. That is a substantial defensive contribution in a game decided by one touchdown.

Connor McLarren had plenty to discuss during the interval. His offense had punted twice before the turnovers, and Blayz Matthews’s two first-quarter sacks had not kept Blackthorn scoreless. Hatterene found Ninjask for a twenty-eight-yard touchdown at 4:59 of the second quarter. The Dragons had a lead, an efficient scoring receiver and the possibility of starting the second half with the ball. Mt. Silver still had a game it could rescue because the defense had limited the damage around those mistakes.

There is a temptation to describe every close playoff win as an exhibition of composure. The first half gives that description some limits. The Reds repeatedly surrendered possessions they had already moved forward. Blackthorn deserves credit for creating and recovering those fumbles, and Mt. Silver deserves credit for the subsequent stops. Both teams had something tangible to regret when they walked off at halftime.
We gave them the ball twice and still had a seven-point game. I suggested we try keeping it for a while. Garshawn seemed to enjoy that part of the discussion.
body.speaker: Connor McLarren

body.text: The kickoff changes the available field

body.alt: Alcremie #12. Crem Ftzpatrik completed eighteen of twenty-five passes for 195 yards. Editorial passing illustration.
body.caption: Crem Ftzpatrik completed eighteen of twenty-five passes for 195 yards. Editorial passing illustration.

body.text: The second half began with Blackthorn’s Ninjask returning the kickoff twenty-five yards to the Dragons’ twenty-six and fumbling. Cranidos recovered for Mt. Silver. In a game with no interceptions, that special-teams turnover gave the home offense its shortest touchdown opportunity and changed the immediate pressure on both sidelines.

Lynch finished the resulting three-play, twenty-six-yard drive with an eight-yard run to the right. The touchdown arrived at 5:15, and Weepinbell’s extra point tied the game. Mt. Silver had needed almost an entire half to reach the scoreboard; it needed less than a minute after the break to erase the deficit. The recovery created the chance, and Lynch converted it into the outcome the Reds had failed to secure on longer first-half possessions.

Blackthorn answered with its best drive of the half. Hatterene led a seven-play, eighty-two-yard possession and found Ninjask deep left for a forty-three-yard touchdown at 3:26. The receiver finished with four catches for 112 yards and both Dragons touchdowns. His return fumble was costly, and his offensive production was essential. A useful account of his afternoon includes both rather than asking one play to explain every snap he took.

The Dragons led 14–7. Their quarterback had thrown two touchdowns without an interception, and the explosive play had restored the lead quickly enough to quiet the home comeback. Mt. Silver’s next response would require a full drive. This time there was no short field from a turnover waiting to simplify the assignment.
Lynch supplies the second response

The Reds traveled sixty-eight yards in six plays. Lynch’s eighteen-yard run on second-and-ten moved them into immediate scoring position; his seven-yard run up the middle finished the possession at 1:51. He had now scored on consecutive Mt. Silver drives, first from a short field and then from a conventional one. Those two circumstances matter because they demonstrate how the rushing production supported the comeback beyond the opening recovery.

Lynch averaged 8.5 yards on his seventeen carries, with a longest run of eighteen. The total came through repeated productive attempts rather than one enormous escape surrounded by losses. Rat Grange added forty yards on seven carries. Together they gave Ftzpatrik a practical way to keep the offense moving without requiring the available quarterback to imitate Hatterene’s previous five-touchdown performance.

Blackthorn’s next possession lasted seven plays and gained eighteen yards before a punt. Mt. Silver took over with thirty-eight seconds remaining in the third quarter. From there the Reds assembled the seventy-one-yard drive that decided the game, mixing their established rushing advantage with timely completions to receivers whose names had appeared less prominently in the pregame argument.

Ftzpatrik opened the fourth quarter with a twenty-four-yard completion to Doduo. Lynch followed with ten rushing yards. Two incompletions then produced third-and-ten, the sort of down on which a narrow game can return to balance. Prinplup caught a fourteen-yard pass to the right. His next reception gained eight, leaving second-and-one. Ftzpatrik found Scep Smith Jr. over the short middle for the one-yard touchdown at 4:32.

body.alt: Prinplup #5. Prinplup converted third-and-ten with a fourteen-yard catch on the winning drive. Editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: Prinplup converted third-and-ten with a fourteen-yard catch on the winning drive. Editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: The final 3:18 belongs to Mt. Silver

Blackthorn had one possession after falling behind. It gained twenty-seven yards in five plays, then punted with 3:18 remaining. The decision placed the next burden on the Dragons’ defense: stop the run, recover the ball and give Hatterene another chance to tie. Mt. Silver instead held possession through the final whistle.

The closing drive covered forty-seven yards in nine recorded plays. Rat Grange gained six yards on consecutive runs around the two-minute warning. Lynch then gained six and seven, moving the chains again before Ftzpatrik’s kneels. The Reds did not need another score. They needed first downs, and the two runners supplied them against a defense that understood precisely what a failed stop would cost.

Mt. Silver finished with twenty first downs to Blackthorn’s ten and 182 rushing yards to the Dragons’ sixty-three. The Reds converted four of six third downs; Blackthorn converted three of eight. Hatterene’s 219 passing yards and two touchdowns kept the visitors competitive, but his offense punted five times. Grovyle, perfect on nine targets at Cinnabar, caught three of eight for eighteen yards here. The previous week’s receiving success offered no automatic solution against a different defense.
Another home game, with a thinner receiving group

The win carries an immediate availability cost. Gregar Jenings is listed for six weeks, and Foo Warner for one. Tic Thorpe, Josh Alakazam and Tony Gyarzalez still have positive recovery counters. Those absences make the next assignment harder, even after Ftzpatrik’s efficient performance established a clear account of how the Reds won this one.

Saffron arrives after beating Lavender 38–9. Mt. Silver won their Week 15 meeting 36–33, and the conference final will require another answer to Archam Manning’s offense and a pass rush that just recorded seven sacks. Lynch gives the Reds a way to control possessions; the available receivers must again finish the difficult downs when the opponent creates them.

Blackthorn exits with a convincing road win at Cinnabar and a seven-point loss to the top seed. The Dragons led this game twice and had enough defensive recoveries to make the first half more profitable than it became. Mt. Silver made the second half its own through three successive touchdown drives, then forty-seven yards of closing offense. That sequence earns the Reds another week and gives the rest of our panel something specific to reconsider.

articles.title: Sunyshore answers for the brothers, then keeps Petalburg off the scoreboard
articles.dek: DeZhaun Watzon throws two touchdowns and Myles Gabite rushes for 134 yards in a 24–10 win with a family connection to Rustboro’s elimination.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Karson Jones supplied the family history before kickoff. Sunyshore quarterback DeZhaun Watzon and Rustboro quarterback Shawn Watzon are brothers. So are Sunyshore runner Myles Gabite and Rustboro runner Philly Gabite. Petalburg had ended Rustboro’s season in the wild-card round, leaving the Starseekers with a divisional opponent and two very personal reasons to remember the previous result.

Sunyshore completed that revenge with a 24–10 victory. Watzon threw two touchdown passes, Gabite ran for 134 yards, and the defense held Petalburg scoreless after halftime. The brothers’ connection gave the matchup its emotional setting; the Starseekers earned the result by sustaining rushing possessions, answering a dangerous interception and keeping the Pride from producing another late playoff comeback.

Jones now takes his team to Mossdeep for the Hoenn–Sinnoh championship. That trip offers its own unfinished business: the Eclipse won their Week 16 meeting 27–3. Sunyshore first had to finish the job in front of it, against a Petalburg team that had already shown how quickly a fourth quarter could become uncomfortable. A fourteen-point lead at the end felt considerably safer than the four-point margin the Starseekers carried into the break.
Watzon finishes a difficult opening drive

There are brothers watching this one who know exactly what that opponent took away last week. We carried that with us. Then you still have to block, finish a run and take care of the football. The family story gets better when you do the work.
body.speaker: Karson Jones

body.text: Petalburg’s defense created genuine obstacles on Sunyshore’s first possession. Delcatty sacked Watzon for four yards, then five more on the following play. The drive nevertheless reached fourth-and-five near the goal line. Jones kept the offense out, and Watzon found Fera LaGatr to the short right for the five-yard touchdown at 1:29 of the first quarter.

That decision deserves to stay attached to its context. The Starseekers had spent eleven plays and more than three minutes moving sixty-four yards. Two sacks had made the ending difficult. The touchdown allowed them to finish the possession at its full value instead of treating the earlier setbacks as a reason to settle. It also established that this game would demand useful short completions from Watzon alongside Gabite’s rushing work.

Ash Rothington had already sacked Iron Valiant on Petalburg’s opening possession. He added another seven-yard sack late in the first quarter as the Pride again punted. Sunyshore took over early in the second and built a seventy-two-yard touchdown drive in nine plays. Watzon completed the two-yard scoring pass to EKTRIK RED at 3:46, and Kayden Lyons’s extra point made it 14–0.

The two touchdowns went to Fera LaGatr and EKTRIK RED rather than the receiver who had caught both scores in the wild-card win. Kobra Khan would contribute differently later. Sunyshore’s available offense found several ways to finish drives despite the continuing absence of 88 Special, whose current injury report still lists fourteen weeks. The result gives the next opponent more than one scoring name to consider.

body.alt: Arbok #19. Kobra Khan scored on a seven-yard fourth-quarter run. Editorial rushing illustration.
body.caption: Kobra Khan scored on a seven-yard fourth-quarter run. Editorial rushing illustration.

body.text: Petalburg makes the last minute count

Petalburg responded with a thirteen-play, seventy-six-yard touchdown drive. Iron Valiant found Glalie for six yards on third-and-six with fifty-one seconds remaining in the half. Sunflora added the extra point. The Pride had converted their longest sustained possession of the half into a touchdown and reduced the deficit to seven before Sunyshore could begin planning a comfortable interval.

The next sequence brought Petalburg even closer. Kabutops sacked Watzon for seven yards, Sunyshore punted, and the Pride took over with twenty-eight seconds remaining. They moved thirty-five yards before Sunflora made a forty-nine-yard field goal with seven seconds left. The Starseekers had led by fourteen; they reached halftime ahead 14–10 after allowing ten points in the closing minute.

For Petalburg, that finish resembled the useful part of its wild-card identity. Iron Valiant’s offense could keep a drive alive, then make another possession count when the opponent left time available. For Sunyshore, it created a practical halftime assignment: protect the ball, keep the ground game productive and stop allowing sacks to hand the visitors quick opportunities. The lead remained theirs, but the direction of the final minute favored the Pride.

Iron Valiant eventually finished sixteen of twenty-eight for 168 yards, one touchdown and one interception. Venomoth led Petalburg with fifty-four receiving yards on two catches. Graveler added thirty-eight on four. Glalie supplied the touchdown reception but gained only fifteen yards on seven carries. The passing game generated enough moments to keep the contest competitive; the rushing game never provided the same sustained support that Gabite gave Sunyshore.
Alexander answers the turnover

The second half began with the danger Sunyshore had wanted to avoid. Watzon threw deep right and Flygon intercepted, returning the ball thirty-four yards. Petalburg was within four points and suddenly had an opportunity to take the lead without crossing the entire field. The Starseekers’ earlier advantage would have become much less useful if that possession had ended in a touchdown.

Scol Alexander answered on third-and-two. Iron Valiant threw deep left, and Alexander intercepted and returned the ball twenty yards out of bounds at 4:45 of the third quarter. The two interceptions arrived less than a minute apart. Sunyshore had surrendered a valuable opportunity, then recovered possession before Petalburg could turn it into points.

Lyons finished the ensuing drive with a forty-two-yard field goal. At 17–10, the Starseekers had restored a seven-point cushion. The sequence is central to the result because the final score can otherwise make the second half seem easier than it was. Petalburg had a chance to change the lead. Alexander’s interception ended it, and the offense and kicking unit converted the response into something measurable.

body.alt: Vigoroth #65. Ash Rothington recorded three sacks in Sunyshore’s win. Imagined postgame portrait.
body.caption: Ash Rothington recorded three sacks in Sunyshore’s win. Imagined postgame portrait.

body.text: Petalburg punted on its next possession after gaining twenty yards. Sunyshore then took over with 1:37 left in the third quarter and assembled another long touchdown drive. This one lasted eleven plays, covered seventy-two yards and crossed into the fourth quarter, giving the Pride fewer remaining possessions in which to recover.
Khan scores, Gabite closes

Delcatty recorded his third sack of the game on first-and-two near the goal line. Sunyshore faced another scoring-area setback and again found a touchdown. Kobra Khan ran left for seven yards at 4:24. The extra point made it 24–10. Khan’s two carries produced twenty-nine yards, including a twenty-two-yard gain elsewhere in the game, and his rushing score provided the separation that his receiving touchdowns had supplied a week earlier.

Rothington then recorded his third sack of Iron Valiant, another seven-yard loss, during Petalburg’s final possession. The Pride punted with 3:10 remaining. They would not get the ball back. Sunyshore’s closing drive covered thirty-nine yards in eight plays, with Gabite providing the first downs that allowed Watzon to finish on kneels.

Gabite gained twelve yards at the two-minute warning and later fourteen on third-and-seven. His nineteen carries produced 134 yards, with a longest gain of fourteen. Like Garshawn Lynch in the other conference, he built a substantial afternoon through repeated successful runs. Those final attempts were particularly valuable: each new set of downs reduced Petalburg’s remaining route back into the game.

Sunyshore finished with 177 rushing yards to Petalburg’s thirty-eight. The Pride actually converted more third downs, five of ten against two of six. That comparison makes the game a useful reminder to examine the possessions around a rate. Sunyshore converted fourth-and-five for an opening touchdown, sustained long scoring drives and received decisive defensive stops. Petalburg’s third-down successes kept it involved, but they could not overcome the second-half scoring drought.
The family story earns another chapter

Watzon’s final line was eleven completions in eighteen attempts for 111 yards, two touchdowns and one interception. Four sacks cost him twenty yards. He had difficult stretches, particularly around halftime and immediately after it, and still completed the throws that finished Sunyshore’s first two scoring drives. Gabite carried the greater share of the yardage burden, while Alexander and Rothington supplied the defensive plays that protected the lead.

The family-revenge framing belongs to Jones’s account of the players’ relationships. The game gives that framing a clear ending: Petalburg eliminated Rustboro, and Sunyshore eliminated Petalburg. The Watzon and Gabite families have a team left in the postseason, and that team has earned a conference-championship trip.

Mossdeep will ask much harder questions of this offense. Sunyshore scored only three points there in the regular season, while the Eclipse have just allowed Dewford three in their playoff opener. Jones arrives with two postseason wins, 240 rushing yards from Gabite across those games and a defense that has allowed sixteen combined points. The brothers’ revenge is complete. The next opponent presents a separate, larger assignment.

articles.title: Five touchdowns for Ninjaskamara, one more game for Mossdeep
articles.dek: The Eclipse beat Dewford 40–3 behind 279 yards from their leading back, then learned Marshall Flock faces a two-week absence.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Ninjaskamara gave Mossdeep five touchdowns and Dewford several different problems. He ran twenty times for 189 yards, caught two passes for ninety more and scored on five of those twenty-two touches. The Eclipse won their playoff opener 40–3, advancing to a conference championship meeting with Sunyshore after a performance that made their earlier three-point win over the Breakers feel very distant.

Mossdeep gained 489 yards, including 247 on the ground. Dewford gained 122. The first three Eclipse possessions all ended in touchdowns, and the defense kept the Breakers out of the end zone throughout. A team that finished the regular season 17–0 returned from its bye with its principal offensive players producing immediately. There was little opportunity for the familiar discussion about whether an extra week off had disturbed anyone's timing.

The result still came with a significant availability change. Marshall Flock is listed for two weeks in the latest injury record, joining Poury Holt, whose counter is now four. The game report does not establish which play caused Flock's injury. Mossdeep heads toward Sunyshore with a dominant new result and a confirmed defensive absence to account for; both belong in the assessment of what this win means.
Three possessions, three touchdowns

Dram Marino completed sixteen of twenty-two passes for 242 yards and three touchdowns without an interception. He found Ninjaskamara for a twenty-four-yard touchdown with 3:40 left in the opening quarter, finishing a seventy-four-yard drive. The back's first scoring contribution came as a receiver, a useful warning for a Dewford defense that would soon spend much of the afternoon dealing with his rushing workload.

Ninjaskamara then scored on a thirty-eight-yard run with 1:23 remaining in the first quarter. That possession covered sixty-six yards. The two opening drives produced fourteen points through different finishes: one passing play to the back and one long carry. Dewford had already been required to defend the full distance twice, without a turnover or a short field doing the preparation work for Mossdeep.

The third scoring drive went eighty-three yards and ended with Marino's ten-yard touchdown pass to Accel BeckhmJr at 3:12 of the second quarter. Vinathorn missed the extra point, leaving the score 20–0. Accel finished with six catches on seven targets for ninety-one yards, the largest receiving total on the team by a single yard. Ninjaskamara's spectacular scoring line had substantial help.

Marino also completed all three of his attempts toward Ninjulio Jones, who gained twenty-five yards. Gronkaludon added twenty-one receiving yards on two catches. Those shorter connections mattered because the offense kept moving between its explosive plays. The opening three drives covered 223 yards in total, a measure of sustained offense as well as individual speed. Dewford could not rely on one successful tackle near midfield to end the immediate danger.
The interruption before halftime

body.alt: Drampa #12, Accelgor #11. Dram Marino and Accel BeckhmJr combined for six completions, ninety-one yards and a touchdown. Imagined sideline conversation.
body.caption: Dram Marino and Accel BeckhmJr combined for six completions, ninety-one yards and a touchdown. Imagined sideline conversation.

body.text: The Breakers did produce a defensive stop before the break. Ambipom sacked Marino during a six-play possession that gained twenty-six yards, and Mossdeep punted. It was the Eclipse's only punt of the game. For Dewford, that sequence offered a brief example of the pressure and down-to-down resistance required to slow the home offense. It arrived after the three touchdown drives had established a twenty-point deficit.

Dewford's own passing game never developed a comparable answer. Frosmoth completed six of fourteen attempts for ninety-two yards, threw an interception and took five sacks for thirty-six lost yards. Those negative plays repeatedly increased the distance the Breakers needed to cover. Against a defense already limiting the rushing attack, that was an expensive way to spend an offensive possession.

Excadrill carried ten times for twenty-seven yards. Watchog added nine on three carries, and the team's final rushing total was thirty yards. Dewford had advanced from the wild-card round by holding Eterna without a touchdown and finishing two short opportunities through Watchog. This game required longer scoring drives, with Mossdeep taking an early lead and giving the Breakers very little ground production to support them.

The difference from the clubs' 24–21 regular-season meeting was therefore visible well beyond the margin. Mossdeep entered halftime ahead 20–0, its defense had kept Dewford from answering any of the early scores, and its offense had repeatedly traveled most of the field. The earlier close game remained a valid reason to take the Breakers seriously before kickoff. The new possessions supplied a much stronger description of this particular afternoon.
A third-down catch becomes sixty-six yards

Ninjaskamara's second receiving touchdown came on third-and-eight with 4:44 left in the third quarter. Marino found him for a sixty-six-yard score. A down on which Dewford could have ended a possession instead became the longest touchdown of the game. The back finished with only two catches, but both reached the end zone and together accounted for ninety yards.

That efficiency makes the receiving line easy to misunderstand if it is read only as a small number of targets or catches. Ninjaskamara's passing-game involvement produced two entire scoring plays, including the third-down answer that widened the lead after halftime. Dewford needed a stop to begin reducing the deficit. Mossdeep extended it before the Breakers could make their next possession a meaningful response to a close score.

Luvrelle Revis intercepted Frosmoth at 3:30 of the third quarter and returned the ball eighteen yards. Ninjaskamara scored on a one-yard run at 2:03, pushing the lead to 34–0. The interception gave Mossdeep another opportunity, and the offense finished it. By then the back had scored twice through the air and twice on the ground, with his final rushing touchdown still ahead.

Derrat Brooks led the defensive pressure with three sacks. Joey Sporeter and Bearon Donald added one apiece. Their contributions gave the pass defense more than a single interception to show for its work. Frosmoth was repeatedly forced to absorb a loss before the Breakers could establish the passing volume required by the score. Dewford's six completions were too few to sustain that pursuit.

body.alt: Raticate #54. Derrat Brooks led Mossdeep with three sacks. Imagined postgame portrait.
body.caption: Derrat Brooks led Mossdeep with three sacks. Imagined postgame portrait.

body.text: Dewford's field goal and Mossdeep's final answer

Camerupt made a thirty-one-yard field goal with twenty-seven seconds remaining in the third quarter, getting Dewford onto the scoreboard at 34–3. The Breakers had avoided a shutout, but the field goal left them needing several additional possessions and almost immediate defensive stops. Mossdeep's next scoring drive removed even that narrow possibility of a late change in the game's character.

Ninjaskamara scored on an eight-yard run with 4:31 left in the fourth quarter. The extra point missed, producing the eventual 40–3 score. Vinathorn finished four-for-six on extra points. Those two misses did not threaten this result, but they are concrete items for a team preparing to play a stronger opponent with a championship berth available. A comfortable margin does not make a failed conversion disappear from the report.
We punted, we missed two kicks, and they got three points. There is enough there for the meeting.
body.speaker: Michael Dorrill

body.text: The coach had just won by thirty-seven, but his three complaints were all specific. Mossdeep can address those details before a game in which one missed conversion or one failed possession could decide the result.

Shawn Mareman helped finish the afternoon with eight carries for fifty-eight yards. On the closing possession he converted third-and-one with a fourteen-yard run and added an eleven-yard gain. Mossdeep covered fifty-four yards while consuming the final 3:38. Ninjaskamara contributed another nine-yard carry during that sequence, bringing his rushing total to 189 without needing another score to underline it.
Sunyshore gets the next opportunity

Mossdeep now hosts the Starseekers, who beat Petalburg 24–10 and have won twice in the playoffs. The Eclipse won the regular-season meeting 27–3. That result and the new Dewford performance make Mossdeep the clear favorite, while Flock's two-week injury entry gives the coming preparation a specific personnel concern. The confirmed absence deserves attention without inventing a replacement lineup or a medical timetable beyond the reported counter.

Dewford leaves with a playoff win over Eterna and a divisional loss in which it could not generate enough offense to challenge the top seed. A full offseason assessment can wait for the season review. The explanation of this game is already substantial: five sacks allowed, thirty rushing yards, no touchdowns and a defense that surrendered three long scoring drives before halftime.

For Mossdeep, Ninjaskamara's 279 scrimmage yards and five touchdowns supplied the headline. Marino's clean passing, Accel's ninety-one receiving yards, Brooks's three sacks and the closing work from Mareman explain the support around it. The Eclipse are one win from the championship game after producing the most complete performance of the divisional round.

art.alt: Mossdeep advanced with a 40–3 win over Dewford. Imagined crowd celebration.

articles.title: Saffron scores the last thirty-eight, ending Lavender’s run
articles.dek: Furfrou’s two interceptions and NeMarcus Tare’s five sacks turn a nine-point deficit into a 38–9 win for the Psi Corps.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender led Saffron 9–0 and had already sacked Archam Manning four times. That is where I would prefer to leave the account. The remaining possessions require considerably more space: Saffron scored thirty-eight unanswered points, Furfrou returned one interception for a touchdown and another to the four-yard line, and NeMarcus Tare finished with five sacks. The Psi Corps won 38–9 and advanced to play at Mt. Silver.

The Wails' nine-game winning streak ended against an opponent that survived a difficult opening and then controlled the passing game on both sides. Manning completed twenty-five of thirty-six attempts for 281 yards and four touchdowns without an interception. Moth Ball finished ten-for-twenty-five for 154 yards, with two interceptions and seven sacks. The difference developed over the game; Lavender's early pressure was both real and insufficient.

Saffron had already beaten Olivine 42–10 in the wild-card round. Its second playoff win followed a similar broad sequence, with an opponent taking an early lead before the Psi Corps produced an extended unanswered response. This time the opening deficit reached nine points, the defensive pressure was more disruptive, and the response included two enormous changes of possession. Lavender had earned the right to make the game uncomfortable. Saffron resolved that discomfort decisively.
EARTHQUAKE!!! makes the opening difficult

EARTHQUAKE!!! recorded four sacks and six pressures for Lavender. The most immediately valuable sack came with 2:30 left in the first quarter, when Manning lost six yards in his own end zone for a safety. The Wails led 2–0. Their pass rush had given them points before either offense had completed a touchdown drive, and Manning's early possessions offered genuine reason for Lavender optimism.

Cheep Caw supplied the touchdown with 4:23 remaining in the second quarter. On fourth-and-one, he scored from the one-yard line, and the extra point made it 9–0. Lavender had converted a short-yardage decision into seven points while its defensive front kept disrupting the favored quarterback. At that moment the Wails had a plausible route through the game: pressure, manageable offensive situations and enough scoring to make each Saffron possession urgent.

That route became harder to follow once the Psi Corps put together a twelve-play, seventy-eight-yard drive. Manning found Bysson Witten for a twelve-yard touchdown on third-and-six with 1:16 left in the half. The conversion was a substantial answer to the earlier sacks. Saffron needed to finish a long possession after falling behind, and the tight end gave Manning a scoring completion on a down Lavender could have used to force a field-goal decision.

The Psi Corps then added a thirty-two-yard field goal with eight seconds remaining before halftime. They went into the break ahead 10–9. Lavender's safety, touchdown and outstanding early pass rush had produced a lead, but not a halftime advantage. Saffron had covered the deficit with ordinary offensive work before the interception returns began to separate the teams in the third quarter.
Two throws, two long returns

body.alt: Ninetales #42. NeMarcus Tare recorded five sacks and eight pressures. Editorial pass-rush illustration.
body.caption: NeMarcus Tare recorded five sacks and eight pressures. Editorial pass-rush illustration.

body.text: Furfrou intercepted Moth Ball and returned the ball forty-nine yards for a touchdown with 5:38 remaining in the third quarter. The score pushed Saffron ahead 17–9. Lavender still trailed by only one possession with a two-point conversion, but the Wails had given away a scoring opportunity and conceded seven points on the same play. Their next meaningful response had to come through an offense already struggling to complete passes consistently.

At 2:37 of the third quarter, Furfrou intercepted another throw and returned it seventy-nine yards, stopping at Lavender's four-yard line. Manning then threw a four-yard touchdown pass to Mothel Irving at 2:18. The two interceptions produced one immediate touchdown and one extremely short scoring opportunity. Furfrou's returns totaled 128 yards, a large amount of field position to concede while trying to recover from a halftime deficit.

The second return made the score 24–9 after the ensuing offensive finish. Lavender now needed more than two ordinary scoring possessions to move ahead, and the time available to build them was shrinking. Moth Ball's final passing line contained ten completions against seven sacks. The Wails could find individual gains, but they could not establish enough reliable passing downs to compensate for the turnovers.

People Eater caught four of six targets for ninety-seven yards, including a forty-seven-yard gain. That was a meaningful receiving contribution in a losing effort. It also accounted for most of Lavender's passing yardage, leaving little production elsewhere to sustain drives after the large play. The Wails converted only two of eleven third downs and punted seven times. Those empty possessions gave Saffron repeated chances to increase the margin.
Tare takes over the pressure story

NeMarcus Tare recorded five sacks and eight pressures, the largest individual defensive line in the game. Chen Norton Jr. added two sacks. Together they accounted for all seven times Moth Ball was taken down. Lavender had introduced the game with EARTHQUAKE!!!'s disruption of Manning; Saffron finished with an even larger sack total and a passing offense that kept scoring after its own difficult start.

The comparison should not turn EARTHQUAKE!!!'s four sacks into a footnote. Those plays directly helped create the early lead, including the safety. They also show the limits of one outstanding performance when the rest of the game develops against a team. Lavender's defender did his job impressively. Saffron recovered well enough to score four offensive touchdowns and a defensive touchdown across the full afternoon.

Hobbes gained fifty-six yards on six rushing attempts, giving Lavender a productive individual rushing line. He also lost a fumble near the end of the third quarter, with Saffron's Jolteon recovering. The Wails finished with three turnovers. A team that had survived Vermilion through Hobbes's spectacular late kickoff return now lost important possessions without receiving another return that could shorten the required comeback.

Lavender gained 220 total yards to Saffron's 345. The Psi Corps' advantage was therefore larger in scoring and possession quality than the raw yardage gap alone describes. The pick-six required no offensive drive, and the second interception left only four yards to cover. Saffron's defense supplied points and field position while its offense avoided giving either back through an interception.

body.alt: Gorebyss #55. Bysson Witten caught two touchdown passes. Editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: Bysson Witten caught two touchdown passes. Editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: Manning keeps finding the end zone

Witten caught a thirteen-yard touchdown with 4:42 remaining in the fourth quarter, his second score of the game. He finished with four catches on six targets for forty-eight yards. HeeDee Lamb added a twenty-one-yard touchdown at 3:40 and led the Psi Corps with seven catches on eight targets for 123 yards. Those final two scores completed the thirty-eight-point response and left Lavender with a twenty-nine-point defeat.

Mothel caught six passes for forty-six yards and a touchdown, while Gengar Pickens added thirty-three receiving yards on four catches. Manning had several productive destinations after the early sacks. Lamb supplied the largest receiving gains, Witten finished twice, and Mothel converted the short opportunity following Furfrou's second return. Each role contributed to an offense that became much harder to interrupt after the opening difficulties.

Dam Skattebo carried ten times for fifty-one yards. Saffron finished with sixty-four rushing yards, a modest total alongside its passing production and defensive scores. Emmitt Smoth remains listed for four weeks in the current injury record. The Psi Corps advanced with Skattebo handling the leading rushing workload, but that confirmed absence continues into the conference championship preparation and deserves to remain part of the matchup discussion.
They had us in trouble, and then everybody started making plays. Everybody. I want that part said properly.
body.speaker: Trent Scarboro

body.text: Travis Scarboro kept his answer shorter: “Nine points won’t do.” Lavender’s promising first half gave way to a second half dominated by Saffron’s scoring and takeaways.
Mt. Silver comes next

Saffron travels to face the Reds, who beat Blackthorn 21–14 and previously won the regular-season meeting between these conference finalists 36–33. The new Psi Corps result adds evidence of a defense that can create substantial scoring opportunities. The four sacks conceded also give Mt. Silver a concrete pressure example to study. A comfortable final margin does not remove the work Saffron needed to do after falling behind.

Lavender's nine straight wins remain an important part of its season, including the wild-card escape against Vermilion. Its divisional elimination came through specific failures: seven sacks allowed, three turnovers, two successful third downs and no second-half points. Saffron answered every one with production. My preferred opening paragraph lasted until the second quarter; the Psi Corps earned the rest of the article.

art.alt: Furfrou #41. Furfrou returned one interception forty-nine yards for a touchdown and another seventy-nine yards. Editorial illustration.

articles.title: Prinplup’s fourteen yards are the part of Mt. Silver’s win I keep replaying
articles.dek: A third-and-ten completion gave the Reds another set of downs on their winning drive. That is a specific job done under pressure.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I want to spend a column on a fourteen-yard catch. Garshawn Lynch earned the larger headline with 145 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Prinplup earned my attention because Mt. Silver faced third-and-ten in the fourth quarter of a tied playoff game, and he caught the pass that kept the winning drive alive. Connor McLarren needed a receiver to complete that particular assignment. Prinplup did it.

The sequence matters. Crem Ftzpatrik had found Doduo for twenty-four yards, and Lynch added ten on the ground. Two incompletions then brought up third-and-ten. With 5:11 remaining, Crem completed the fourteen-yard pass to Prinplup. The receiver followed it with an eight-yard catch, and Scep Smith Jr. finished the drive with the one-yard touchdown reception that made the score 21–14.

Those are twenty-two receiving yards from Prinplup on consecutive completions during the decisive possession. His whole game was four catches on four targets for twenty-nine yards. Read that final total without the down and distance and it looks like a modest contribution. Put the catches back into their actual sequence and you can see why I am taking up space on the page.

Mt. Silver had already lost two first-half fumbles after completions. Gregar Jenings gained twenty-five yards before losing the ball; Scep gained six before his fumble. Blackthorn punted after both. The Reds had received two chances to recover from failed possession security, and they reached halftime down seven. By the fourth quarter, another wasted opportunity would have been particularly expensive. Prinplup's catches helped turn the next important series into the lead.

I am not assigning him a secret route adjustment that the play record does not show. The observable work is enough: a completed fourteen-yard pass on third-and-ten, then another eight yards. We can evaluate the conversion without writing an imaginary coaching clinic around it. I get impatient with that temptation because it often buries the useful football beneath a pile of confident terminology.

McLarren put it plainly in our interview: “At third-and-ten you need somebody to give the quarterback a completion that actually gets ten. He gave us fourteen. That changes the rest of the drive.” The statement fits the situation exactly. A short catch and a tackle could have left Mt. Silver making a fourth-down decision. The recorded catch gave the Reds a new set of downs and kept the touchdown available.

Saffron now makes that kind of contribution more valuable. The Psi Corps recorded seven sacks against Lavender. A pressure play can create a difficult down even on a possession that began well. Mt. Silver also has Gregar newly listed for six weeks, with Tony Gyarzalez still at three. The available receiving group has to keep completing jobs that would be easier to distribute across a healthier roster.

That does not mean Prinplup should automatically become the first option on every passing down. Four successful targets do not establish a universal prescription. They establish that the receiver delivered when this game required him. I want the preparation to preserve the useful evidence: which available players have actually converted the situations the next opponent is likely to create?

Lynch will remain central to the Reds' offense, and he should. Mt. Silver also needs a passing answer when the first two downs fail. Prinplup supplied one at 5:11 of the fourth quarter, then helped move the ball again on the next completion. Give the player credit for the specific work. McLarren's team is still playing because enough of those assignments were completed before Blackthorn could get the ball back.

art.alt: Prinplup #5. Prinplup’s third-down contribution is the subject of Mara’s column. Imagined meeting-room scene.

articles.title: EARTHQUAKE!!! played well enough to deserve a separate sentence
articles.dek: Lavender’s season ended with a heavy defeat. Four sacks and a safety still describe an excellent individual performance.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: EARTHQUAKE!!! recorded four sacks against Saffron, including the sack that produced Lavender's opening safety. I would like that fact to survive the week. The Wails lost 38–9, their nine-game winning streak ended, and the offense had a miserable second half. All of those things are true. So is the excellence of the player who made Archam Manning's first possessions difficult.

The safety came with 2:30 left in the first quarter. Manning lost six yards in his own end zone, and Lavender took a 2–0 lead. By the time Cheep Caw scored from the one on fourth-and-one in the second quarter, the Wails had a nine-point advantage and substantial defensive pressure behind it. Anyone watching only the opening had sensible grounds for thinking an upset was possible.

I had picked Lavender to win, which makes me an interested witness. It also makes the eventual account rather inconvenient. Saffron scored the next thirty-eight points. Manning finished with four touchdown passes and no interceptions, while Moth Ball took seven sacks and threw two interceptions. I can describe EARTHQUAKE!!!'s work accurately without using it to excuse the rest of my forecast.

That separation is the point I want to keep. A lopsided final score can make an individual contribution disappear from the conversation, especially when the losing club is eliminated and everyone begins looking toward the next matchup. Lavender's defender produced four sacks and six pressures. He supplied two points directly and helped make the first half competitive. The team needed several other things to go well afterward, and they did not.

Travis Scarboro was brief when I asked about the performance: “Four sacks. He gave us a chance.” That is enough praise to be useful. Travis did not need to turn the answer into a claim that the defense had solved Saffron or that the final margin was unfair. The early pressure created an opportunity. The opponent recovered and won decisively.

NeMarcus Tare's five sacks for Saffron will receive more attention because they came in a victory and helped send the Psi Corps to the conference championship. They deserve that attention. The two performances can be assessed together without requiring one to cancel the other. Tare had the larger sack total, Saffron had the better full game, and EARTHQUAKE!!! still played an outstanding individual afternoon.

Lavender has enough specific problems to discuss without inventing another. The Wails converted two of eleven third downs, turned the ball over three times and scored no points after their second-quarter touchdown. Those failures explain the elimination much more directly than any suggestion that every member of a losing team must have performed poorly. The defensive line's early work belongs on the other side of that review.

I also want to resist declaring the entire season settled by the latest margin. Nine consecutive wins preceded this defeat, including the extraordinary finish against Vermilion. That history does not reduce Saffron's victory, and it does not turn the divisional game into a narrow escape. It gives us the appropriate amount of season to remember before the full review is written.

There will be time to discuss what Lavender should change. This week, one part of the record is already clear enough to state without a committee meeting: EARTHQUAKE!!! reached Manning four times, forced a safety and helped give the Wails a nine-point lead. The player earned credit even though the team could not keep the lead. I intend to leave that credit in print.

art.alt: Dugtrio #24. EARTHQUAKE!!! recorded four sacks in Lavender’s loss. Imagined postgame portrait.

articles.title: Karson should make Mossdeep wait for the ball
articles.dek: Gabite’s closing carries give Sunyshore a concrete starting point for an upset plan. A passing race would ask the Starseekers to win the wrong contest.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Myles Gabite gained twelve yards at the two-minute mark and fourteen more on third-and-seven with 1:51 left against Petalburg. Sunyshore then knelt out a 24–10 win. Karson Jones should put that sequence at the front of the conference championship meeting. His best chance against Mossdeep begins with a runner who can turn a competitive possession into several more minutes without Dram Marino on the field.

I picked all four divisional winners. This entitles me to one paragraph of professional serenity before the next round makes me look foolish again. I was also the only writer on our panel to take Mt. Silver, largely because Garshawn Lynch gave the Reds a way to sustain offense without requiring an injured passing group to win every exchange. Gabite gives Sunyshore a related argument, although Mossdeep is a considerably harder opponent.

The Starseekers have received 240 rushing yards from Gabite in two playoff games. He carried nineteen times for 134 against Petalburg, with a longest gain of fourteen. That is repeated production across a substantial workload. Sunyshore does not have to imagine that he can keep a possession moving; he has just supplied the carries that ended an opponent's season without giving it another meaningful offensive chance.

The difficulty is arriving at the closing minutes with a lead. Mossdeep scored touchdowns on its first three possessions against Dewford, gaining seventy-four, sixty-six and eighty-three yards on those drives. Karson cannot simply announce an intention to run and expect Marino to cooperate. Sunyshore needs early stops, successful first downs and touchdown finishes. The rushing plan has to produce points as well as elapsed time.

That is still a more persuasive starting point than asking DeZhaun Watzon to trade passing touchdowns all afternoon. Watzon threw two against Petalburg, but he also took four sacks and threw an interception. His final passing total was 111 yards. Marino's latest game produced 242 yards and three touchdowns without a pick, supported by ninety-one receiving yards from Accel BeckhmJr and two scoring catches from Ninjaskamara.

Jones's view was direct: “Myles has earned the work. We have to give him possessions where that work can count.” I agree with the wording. A runner cannot protect a lead his team never establishes, and he cannot compensate indefinitely for drives ruined by sacks or turnovers. Sunyshore's preparation has to connect Gabite's workload to the defensive stops and efficient passing that keep the score manageable.

Kobra Khan gives the plan another useful detail. He ran for twenty-nine yards on two attempts against Petalburg, including the seven-yard touchdown that extended the lead in the fourth quarter. Sunyshore's ground production therefore included a finishing contribution beyond Gabite's steady gains. A defense preparing for the main runner still has to account for the other players who have actually produced when given the ball.

Mossdeep's defensive result against Dewford prevents me from turning this into an upset prediction. The Breakers gained thirty rushing yards, and the Eclipse recorded five sacks. Sunyshore's 27–3 regular-season loss at Mossdeep is another substantial warning. My round pick remains Mossdeep 28–24, closer than my colleagues' forecasts because I expect Gabite to give the visitors enough sustained offense to stay involved.

Karson has earned a conference championship appearance through two playoff wins and a defense that has conceded sixteen total points in them. He does not need to apologize for entering as the underdog. He does need to make the game resemble the situations his best players have already handled. Give Gabite useful downs, finish the drives, and make Mossdeep wait through actual first downs instead of a hopeful speech about controlling the clock.

art.alt: Garchomp #99. Dorian argues for sustained rushing possessions through Myles Gabite. Imagined practice scene.

articles.title: Granbull and Dracozolt lead a defensive-line board with distinct jobs
articles.dek: Twelve visible prospects separate into interior, edge and nose-tackle options; the combine adds context to the reported ranges.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: University of Pyrite's Granbull and Turffield State's Dracozolt lead this defensive-line board. Granbull has the highest visible range among the twelve selected prospects at 65–93. Dracozolt follows at 64–92 and adds nineteen bench repetitions, a 4.82 forty and a 6.85 cone. The first choice depends in part on whether a club is seeking a defensive tackle or an edge player; the listed positions matter.

Dracozolt's movement tests make the edge evaluation particularly interesting. Solaceon's Heatmor has nineteen bench reps too, alongside a thirty-seven-inch vertical and a 6.80 cone, but a lower 53–81 range. Sonia's separate Heatmor runs 4.86 with a 6.79 cone and fourteen bench reps. Those are different combinations of reported range, strength and movement, not interchangeable versions of the same prospect.

The interior group has a wider gap between the leading candidate and the next name. University of Mossdeep's Loudred carries a 51–79 range at defensive tackle. Four listed nose tackles follow later on this board with narrower ranges. A team should compare those players against the job it actually needs filled rather than treating every defensive lineman as an equivalent answer to a sack total.

The divisional round offered several reminders that pressure can matter without establishing a complete scouting method. NeMarcus Tare recorded five sacks, EARTHQUAKE!!! four, and Derrat Brooks three. These are performances by established league players. They do not prove that a prospect with a similar species or a particular combine number will reproduce the same result. The college board below uses the visible scouting record for each individual.

No final draft order is assigned here, and the range endpoints are not secretly revealed current ratings. The judgments identify which prospects I would examine first and why. The next useful step for a club is to reduce uncertainty about its intended role, especially when choosing between a broad-range edge player and a more narrowly reported nose tackle.

prospects.name: Granbull
prospects.analysis: Granbull leads this board with a 65–93 visible range, a 5.01 forty and a 6.97 cone. University of Pyrite’s defensive tackle gives me the strongest reported range among these twelve.
prospects.concern: Fifteen bench repetitions do not establish a dominant strength advantage.
prospects.projection: First interior option on this board, with the broad range still requiring further evaluation.

prospects.name: Dracozolt
prospects.analysis: Turffield State’s Dracozolt pairs a 64–92 range with nineteen bench reps, a 4.82 forty and a 6.85 cone. I prefer this movement profile among the leading edge candidates.
prospects.concern: The range remains wide, and testing does not reveal a complete pass-rush repertoire.
prospects.projection: The leading defensive end here and a serious alternative to Granbull for a team prioritizing the edge.

prospects.name: Heatmor
prospects.analysis: Solaceon’s Heatmor has a 53–81 range, nineteen bench reps and a thirty-seven-inch vertical. The 6.80 cone is another reason to keep the prospect high.
prospects.concern: The reported range sits below the leading pair despite the attractive testing.
prospects.projection: An early alternative among this selected group if the top two are unavailable.

prospects.name: Carnivine
prospects.analysis: Agate’s Carnivine combines a 52–80 range with sixteen bench reps and a 6.96 cone. The profile earns a place near the top of the second group.
prospects.concern: A 5.03 forty offers less straight-line speed than Dracozolt.
prospects.projection: A developmental edge candidate whose specific role needs further evaluation.

prospects.name: Cranidos
prospects.analysis: Vermilion Metro’s Cranidos has the same 52–80 range and nineteen bench reps. Strength testing makes the comparison with Carnivine worth a close look.
prospects.concern: The 5.07 forty does not suggest the same movement profile as the fastest edge candidates.
prospects.projection: A second-group option for clubs weighing strength more heavily in their intended role.

prospects.name: Carnivine
prospects.analysis: South Paldea’s Carnivine is a separate prospect, with a 51–79 range, seventeen bench reps and a 5.00 forty. Keep the school and identity distinct from Agate’s player.
prospects.concern: The 7.02 cone is slower than several nearby alternatives.
prospects.projection: A middle-board edge option with a broad unresolved range.

prospects.name: Loudred
prospects.analysis: University of Mossdeep’s Loudred brings a 51–79 range at defensive tackle, with a 5.03 forty and a 7.00 cone. It is the next interior candidate after Granbull on this list.
prospects.concern: Fifteen bench reps do not remove uncertainty about the intended interior job.
prospects.projection: An interior alternative when the strongest range is no longer available.

prospects.name: Heatmor
prospects.analysis: Sonia’s Heatmor has a 50–78 range but a 4.86 forty and a 6.79 cone. That movement is the clearest reason to investigate a prospect below several peers by range.
prospects.concern: Fourteen bench reps give a different strength profile from Solaceon’s Heatmor.
prospects.projection: A movement-oriented edge option, with technical and role questions still open.

prospects.name: Geodude
prospects.analysis: Hauoli State’s Geodude is listed at nose tackle with a 50–50 range. The narrow reported interval distinguishes this evaluation from the wide-range defensive ends.
prospects.concern: A 5.23 forty, 7.18 cone and thirteen bench reps provide no basis for projecting unseen traits.
prospects.projection: A role-specific nose-tackle candidate evaluated on the known range.

prospects.name: Geodude
prospects.analysis: Oreburgh State’s Geodude has a 49–49 range and fifteen bench reps, with a 5.17 forty. The testing provides a useful comparison within the nose-tackle group.
prospects.concern: A fixed reported range should not be converted into an assumed development ceiling.
prospects.projection: A nose-tackle alternative with a slightly stronger bench result than the Hauoli prospect.

prospects.name: Geodude
prospects.analysis: University of Goldenrod’s Geodude also has a 49–49 range, with fourteen bench reps and a 5.18 forty. This is a third distinct player, not a repeated listing.
prospects.concern: The 7.13 cone is a testing result, not proof of game-level penetration.
prospects.projection: Another role-specific option in a tightly grouped nose-tackle set.

prospects.name: Roggenrola
prospects.analysis: Couriway’s Roggenrola closes the board with a 49–49 range and a thirty-one-inch vertical. The species and school distinguish the prospect from the three Geodude entries.
prospects.concern: Twelve bench reps and a 7.26 cone leave the testing case behind several nearby players.
prospects.projection: A later nose-tackle consideration when the role and remaining options justify it.

articles.title: Mt. Silver’s rushing answer meets Saffron’s expanding passing attack
articles.dek: The Reds won the first meeting 36–33. The rematch brings a new injury to Gregar Jenings and a Psi Corps defense coming off seven sacks.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Mt. Silver and Saffron have already played a three-point game with sixty-nine combined points. The Reds won that Week 15 meeting 36–33. They now host the conference championship after a very different kind of victory, beating Blackthorn 21–14 with three second-half touchdowns and a closing possession that denied the Dragons another chance. Saffron arrives after scoring thirty-eight unanswered points against Lavender.

Both clubs finished the regular season 14–3. Mt. Silver earned the top seed with 481 points scored and 206 allowed; Saffron scored 597 and conceded 138. The Reds' earlier head-to-head win deserves direct weight, while the broader scoring records favor the Psi Corps. Those two pieces of evidence produce a competitive matchup without requiring the latest playoff margin to erase the season that preceded it.

The most significant new personnel detail is Gregar Jenings's six-week injury entry. He caught one pass for twenty-five yards against Blackthorn, then lost a fumble on that play. The injury record does not establish the injury's timing or connect it to that reception. It does establish another absence in a Mt. Silver passing group already dealing with several positive recovery counters.
Lynch gives the Reds a complete offensive argument

Garshawn Lynch carried seventeen times for 145 yards and two touchdowns against Blackthorn. His eighteen-yard and seven-yard runs helped finish the tying touchdown drive in the third quarter, and he continued contributing as the Reds built their winning possession. Mt. Silver gained 182 rushing yards as a team, with Rat Grange adding forty on seven carries. The rushing attack supplied both substantial gains and useful work between them.

That production made the available passing game easier to support. Crem Ftzpatrik completed eighteen of twenty-five passes for 195 yards and one touchdown without an interception. He did not need to match Hatterene's previous five-touchdown performance to win. The Reds combined Lynch's larger gains with shorter completions and kept possession through the final 3:18 after taking the lead.

Saffron allowed Hobbes fifty-six rushing yards on six carries. That individual line gives Mt. Silver a reason to test the run, although Lavender's overall offense failed to turn it into enough scoring. Lynch's divisional workload was much larger, and the Reds will want enough competitive possessions to keep using him. A large early deficit would make the balance that worked against Blackthorn more difficult to preserve.

The prior 36–33 meeting shows that Mt. Silver has already found enough offense to beat this opponent. The new preview cannot assume the same distribution of touches or the same available lineup. It can retain the result while asking whether Lynch and the current receiving group can reproduce the required scoring. That is a more useful question than treating either the earlier win or Saffron's latest margin as conclusive by itself.
The receiving group has another absence

Gregar joins a list that includes Tony Gyarzalez at three weeks, Josh Alakazam at two and Tic Thorpe at one. Foo Warner has a new one-week entry. Vibrava remains at three, Ariados at eight and Medicham at two. These reported counters describe the current record. They do not establish a medical return date or permit us to place a cleared player into a starting role before the lineup is known.

The available receivers nevertheless produced several important answers against Blackthorn. Plusico Buress caught five passes for sixty-two yards. Prinplup caught all four targets for twenty-nine, including a fourteen-yard conversion on third-and-ten during the winning drive. Scep Smith Jr. finished that possession with a one-yard touchdown catch after contributing other short receptions earlier in the game.

Prinplup's third-down play is especially relevant to this matchup. Saffron's pass rush can create the kind of difficult down that forces a quarterback to use an available receiver outside the most prominent names. Mt. Silver has just completed such a pass in a close playoff game. One conversion does not promise another, but it provides actual evidence that the current group can finish a demanding passing situation.

The two lost first-half fumbles against Blackthorn remain a concern. Gregar lost the ball after his twenty-five-yard catch, and Scep after a six-yard reception. The Dragons punted after both takeaways, allowing the Reds to reach halftime down only seven. Saffron has just demonstrated a much more damaging response to turnovers. Mt. Silver cannot reasonably build its preparation around receiving the same reprieve twice.
Manning recovered from a difficult opening

Archam Manning took four sacks against Lavender, including the sack that produced a safety. Saffron fell behind 9–0 before its offense completed a twelve-play, seventy-eight-yard touchdown drive. Manning then helped take a 10–9 halftime lead and finished with 281 passing yards, four touchdowns and no interceptions. The recovery matters because Mt. Silver's defensive pressure does not have to be hypothetical to affect the forecast.

Blayz Matthews recorded two sacks and four pressures against Blackthorn. He gives the Reds a recent example of disruption to carry into preparation for Manning. Lavender's EARTHQUAKE!!! supplied four sacks and six pressures, so there is also direct evidence that Saffron's protection can be beaten. The challenge is maintaining enough pressure across the game while preventing Manning's successful completions from becoming a sequence of touchdowns.

HeeDee Lamb caught seven passes on eight targets for 123 yards and a touchdown against Lavender. Bysson Witten added forty-eight yards and two touchdowns on four catches, while Mothel Irving caught six passes for forty-six yards and another score. Gengar Pickens contributed four catches for thirty-three. Manning's scoring options are therefore spread across several players with recent production, including the receiver who finished the long drive that began Saffron's comeback.

Mt. Silver limited Grovyle to three catches for eighteen yards after his nine-catch, 135-yard wild-card performance. It still allowed Ninjask 112 receiving yards and two touchdowns, including a forty-three-yard score. The Reds have evidence of reducing one productive receiver without fully containing the entire passing game. Saffron's several established targets make that distinction central to the championship matchup.
Saffron can score through its defense

Furfrou intercepted Moth Ball twice, returning the first forty-nine yards for a touchdown and the second seventy-nine yards to the four-yard line. Saffron's offense promptly finished the short field after the second return. Those plays helped turn a one-point halftime lead into a substantial third-quarter advantage, and they made Lavender's passing difficulties more expensive than a sequence of ordinary incompletions.

NeMarcus Tare recorded five sacks and eight pressures, with Chen Norton Jr. adding two sacks. Mt. Silver's offense must therefore account for both the rush and the possibility of a damaging throw while trying to escape it. Crem's interception-free divisional game is a positive starting point. The Reds still lost two possessions through fumbles, and Saffron's defense has just converted opponent mistakes into immediate scoring opportunities.

The Psi Corps also recovered Hobbes's third-quarter fumble. Their three takeaways came in a game in which their own quarterback threw no interceptions. Predicting another two-interception afternoon from one defender would go beyond the evidence. Recognizing the cost of giving this offense extra possessions is a straightforward conclusion from what it just did with them.

Emmitt Smoth remains listed for four weeks, leaving Saffron with a continuing backfield absence. Dam Skattebo carried ten times for fifty-one yards against Lavender, after a larger rushing contribution in the wild-card win. The Psi Corps can still get useful ground production, but their latest scoring was driven by Manning's four touchdown passes and the defensive returns. Mt. Silver will have to defend that demonstrated emphasis while respecting the available rushing option.
Possession count and finishing drives

The Reds' final possession against Blackthorn consumed 3:18 and gained forty-seven yards. Rat Grange opened with consecutive six-yard carries, and Lynch added six and seven before the closing kneel-downs. Mt. Silver never had to make a final defensive stop after the Dragons' last punt. A similar finish would be extremely valuable against Manning, provided the Reds can reach the late game with a lead to protect.

Saffron's response to Lavender suggests why reaching that position is the difficult part. The Psi Corps scored on a long drive before halftime, added a late field goal, then used defensive returns and further touchdown passes to extend the lead. They have several ways to change the score within a small number of possessions. Mt. Silver's rushing success needs to produce touchdowns often enough to keep that variety from deciding the game early.

The earlier three-point meeting supports a close forecast. So does Mt. Silver's ability to win a playoff game with its current quarterback and receiving options. Saffron's stronger full-season scoring record, two convincing playoff wins and several productive passing destinations give the visitors my narrow preference. Gregar's new absence reduces the Reds' room for another lost receiving contribution during the game.

I pick Saffron 31, Mt. Silver 27. Lynch should keep the home offense moving, and the Reds have shown enough third-down execution to make the final possessions important. I expect Manning's ability to find different finishers to create one additional touchdown opportunity, with Saffron avoiding the turnovers that would let Mt. Silver spend the closing minutes running out another four-point lead.
